cards.back: Sufficient in quality or quantity for a particular purpose. "The hotel provided adequate facilities for the conference." Common collocations: adequate supply, adequate resources, perfectly adequate.

To distribute or set aside resources for a particular purpose. "The government decided to allocate more funding to public education." Common collocations: allocate resources, allocate funds, allocate time.
To expect or predict that something will happen. "Analysts anticipate a sharp rise in oil prices next quarter." Common collocations: widely anticipated, anticipate problems, anticipate demand.

To evaluate or estimate the nature, quality, or importance of something. "Teachers need to assess each student's progress regularly." Common collocations: assess the impact, assess the situation, accurately assess.

A condition or fact that affects a situation. "Under no circumstance should you share your password with others." Common collocations: under the circumstances, exceptional circumstances, difficult circumstances.

To make up for something unwelcome by providing something good, or to pay someone for work or loss. "The company agreed to compensate workers for the overtime hours." Common collocations: compensate for losses, compensate employees, fully compensate.
A part or element of a larger whole. "Teamwork is a key component of success in any organization." Common collocations: key component, essential component, major component.

Including all or nearly all elements or aspects of something; thorough. "The report provides a comprehensive overview of the current housing crisis." Common collocations: comprehensive review, comprehensive plan, comprehensive guide.

To bring something to an end, or to arrive at a judgement after reasoning. "The researchers concluded that diet plays a significant role in heart health." Common collocations: conclude an agreement, reasonably conclude, conclude by saying.

Following as a result or effect of something. "The storm and consequent flooding caused widespread damage across the region." Common collocations: consequent upon, consequent changes, consequent increase.
A limitation or restriction on something. "Budget constraints forced the team to reduce the scope of the project." Common collocations: time constraints, financial constraints, impose constraints.

Prolonged public disagreement or heated debate about a subject. "The new policy sparked considerable controversy among parents and teachers." Common collocations: cause controversy, political controversy, surrounded by controversy.

Of great importance; critical to the outcome of something. "Good communication skills are crucial for career advancement." Common collocations: play a crucial role, crucial factor, absolutely crucial.

To decrease in quantity, importance, or quality; or to politely refuse. "The population of wild bees has declined dramatically over the past decade." Common collocations: sharp decline, decline in quality, steady decline.

To show clearly by giving proof or evidence; to display or explain how something works. "The experiment was designed to demonstrate the effects of gravity on plant growth." Common collocations: clearly demonstrate, demonstrate ability, demonstrate understanding.

To make or become less in size, importance, or value. "Nothing should diminish the significance of this historic achievement." Common collocations: greatly diminished, diminish the value, diminish in importance.

Recognizably different in nature or clearly separate from something else. "There are two distinct approaches to solving this mathematical problem." Common collocations: quite distinct, distinct possibility, distinct advantage.

To have a commanding influence or control over something. "Large corporations continue to dominate the global technology market." Common collocations: dominate the market, dominate the conversation, dominate the landscape.

Involving many carefully arranged parts or details; or (verb) to add more detail. "Could you elaborate on the main points of your research proposal?" Common collocations: elaborate plan, elaborate further, elaborate on details.
To come into view or existence; to become apparent or known. "New evidence has emerged that challenges the original theory." Common collocations: emerge from, emerge as a leader, newly emerged.

To unexpectedly meet or face a situation, problem, or person. "Students often encounter difficulties when writing their first academic essay." Common collocations: encounter problems, encounter resistance, close encounter.
To rise and fall irregularly in number or amount. "House prices tend to fluctuate depending on supply and demand." Common collocations: fluctuate widely, fluctuate between, prices fluctuate.
Forming a necessary base or core; of central importance. "Access to clean water is a fundamental human right." Common collocations: fundamental change, fundamental principles, fundamental difference.
To put a decision, plan, or agreement into effect. "The school plans to implement a new anti-bullying policy next term." Common collocations: implement a strategy, implement changes, fully implement.

A likely consequence of something; or a suggestion of something not directly expressed. "The findings have serious implications for public health policy." Common collocations: wider implications, practical implications, by implication.
Certain to happen; unavoidable. "With rising sea levels, some degree of coastal flooding is inevitable." Common collocations: seem inevitable, inevitable consequence, virtually inevitable.
Existing as a natural or permanent quality of something. "There are inherent risks associated with any form of surgery." Common collocations: inherent risk, inherent weakness, inherent in the system.
To hinder, restrain, or prevent an action or process. "Fear of failure can inhibit creativity and innovation." Common collocations: inhibit growth, inhibit development, inhibit the ability.

A conception of or belief about something; an idea or opinion. "The notion that money alone brings happiness has been widely challenged." Common collocations: popular notion, preconceived notion, reject the notion.

To become aware of something through the senses or to interpret something in a particular way. "Many people perceive online learning as less effective than traditional education." Common collocations: widely perceived, perceive as a threat, perceived benefits.

A fact or situation that is observed to exist or happen, especially one whose cause is in question. "Global warming is a phenomenon that affects every continent on Earth." Common collocations: natural phenomenon, cultural phenomenon, widespread phenomenon.

Present as the strongest or main element; having the greatest influence. "English is the predominant language used in international scientific publications." Common collocations: predominant factor, predominant role, predominant view.

The possibility or likelihood of some future event occurring; or a potential opportunity. "The prospect of finding a well-paid job motivates many students to study abroad." Common collocations: job prospects, future prospects, exciting prospect.
Unwilling and hesitant; not eager to do something. "Many employees were reluctant to adopt the new software system." Common collocations: reluctant to change, seem reluctant, reluctant participant.

To attempt to find or obtain something; to try to achieve a goal. "Many young professionals seek opportunities to work in international organizations." Common collocations: seek advice, seek approval, seek employment.

To imitate the appearance or character of something; to create a model of a process. "Computer programs can simulate real-world weather patterns with great accuracy." Common collocations: simulate conditions, simulate an environment, closely simulate.

Coming after something in time; following. "The initial study and subsequent research confirmed the original findings." Common collocations: subsequent events, subsequent analysis, in subsequent years.

To maintain something at a certain level over a period of time; to support or endure. "It is difficult to sustain economic growth without investing in education." Common collocations: sustain growth, sustain interest, sustain damage.

To experience or be subjected to something, typically something unpleasant or demanding. "Patients must undergo a thorough medical examination before the procedure." Common collocations: undergo surgery, undergo training, undergo changes.
Having a sound basis in logic or fact; legally or officially acceptable. "You need a valid passport to travel internationally." Common collocations: valid argument, valid reason, perfectly valid.

To regard something as being caused by a particular factor; or a quality of someone. "Researchers attribute the decline in bee populations to pesticide use." Common collocations: attribute success to, key attribute, positive attribute.

To get rid of something; or to make someone inclined to a particular attitude. "Residents must dispose of household waste according to local regulations." Common collocations: dispose of waste, dispose of properly, well-disposed.
Clearly seen or understood; obvious. "It was evident from the results that the new treatment was highly effective." Common collocations: clearly evident, self-evident, immediately evident.

About to happen or appear; or willing to reveal information. "Details of the forthcoming changes will be published next week." Common collocations: forthcoming election, forthcoming publication, not very forthcoming.

To combine one thing with another so that they become a whole. "Schools are working to integrate technology into everyday classroom activities." Common collocations: fully integrate, integrate into society, integrate systems.

Of a minimum amount, quantity, or degree; very small or slight. "The project was completed with minimal disruption to daily operations." Common collocations: minimal effort, minimal impact, keep to a minimal level.

To continue firmly in an action or belief despite difficulty or opposition. "Unemployment problems persist in many rural areas despite government efforts." Common collocations: persist in doing, problems persist, persist over time.

Income generated from business operations, sales, or other sources. "Tourism is the primary source of revenue for many island nations." Common collocations: generate revenue, annual revenue, revenue growth.

To cause an event or situation to happen or exist; a factor that initiates a process. "The economic crisis triggered a wave of protests across the country." Common collocations: trigger a response, trigger a debate, trigger an alarm.

To be the cause or basis of something; to lie beneath. "Several factors underlie the recent increase in youth unemployment." Common collocations: underlie the problem, underlying cause, underlying principle.
